reason: The sources provide over 10 cross-verified claims confirming that passing a supermassive black hole's event horizon occurs without local drama or instant crushing forces.
story: In 1916, while serving on the front lines of World War I, German physicist Karl Schwarzschild solved Albert Einstein's equations of general relativity. He revealed that compressing mass into a small enough radius creates an event horizon—a mathematical point of no return where escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Popular culture depicts the event horizon as a destructive cosmic wall, but physics tells a very different story. If you fell into a giant supermassive black hole, such as the one at the center of a galaxy, you would experience no sudden jolts, crushing forces, or dramatic flashes upon crossing the boundary. Because space curvature at a large horizon is gentle, you would glide right through intact. Only an outside observer sees you slow down and fade away. Crushing tidal forces and spaghettification wouldn't strike until you traveled much deeper toward the central singularity.
angle: Crossing the edge of a giant supermassive black hole would feel completely unremarkable—you wouldn't notice or feel anything special at the boundary.

claims.claim: The event horizon is the outer boundary of a black hole where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein's general relativity field equations in 1916, defining the radius of the event horizon.
The event horizon is not a physical barrier, but a mathematically defined surface marking a point of no return.
Inside an event horizon, the escape velocity required to escape gravity exceeds the speed of light.
If the Sun were compressed into a black hole, its event horizon radius would be approximately 3 kilometers (1.86 to 1.9 miles).
If Earth were compressed into a black hole, its event horizon radius would be approximately 9 millimeters (0.35 inches).
Austrian physicist Wolfgang Rindler coined the term 'event horizon'.
To an outside observer, an object approaching an event horizon appears to slow down and redden over time due to gravitational redshift.
A distant observer will never see an infalling object actually cross the event horizon; it simply fades to invisibility.
An observer falling into a supermassive black hole would feel no crushing forces or notice anything unusual upon crossing the event horizon.
In stellar-mass black holes, tidal forces tear an explorer apart via spaghettification before they reach the event horizon.
In supermassive black holes, spaghettification occurs deep inside the event horizon near the central singularity.
At the center of a black hole lies a singularity of infinite density where current laws of physics break down.
A supermassive black hole containing millions of solar masses resides at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.

disputed: The exact year Wolfgang Rindler coined 'event horizon' is given as the 1950s in S1 and specifically 1956 in S4; a script should state 'in the 1950s'.
The mass of Sagittarius A* is specified as 4.3 million solar masses in S2 and about 4 million in S4; a script should attribute or say 'over four million solar masses'.
The Sun's Schwarzschild radius is precisely 3 km (1.86–1.9 miles) in S1 and S2, but approximated as about 2 miles (3.2 km) in S4.
